scenes.name: Soul jazz: órgano Hammond y guitarra
scenes.author: Ted Gioia
scenes.desc: El hard bop impregnado de gospel y rhythm and blues que Alfred Lion no quería publicar y acabó explotando: ritmos binarios y cuaternarios guturales, llamada y respuesta, blues, la herencia de los tenores tejanos y de Kansas City y las batallas de saxos (Lockjaw Davis y Johnny Griffin). Su voz es el órgano Hammond B-3: tras Bill Doggett y Wild Bill Davis, Jimmy Smith lo impone en Blue Note con blues de veinte minutos («The Sermon»); le siguen Jimmy McGriff, Jack McDuff, Shirley Scott o Groove Holmes, y Larry Young lo lleva a Coltrane y a la fusión de Lifetime. En la guitarra, Kenny Burrell (Midnight Blue) y Wes Montgomery, autodidacta que toca con el pulgar y en octavas y acaba vendiendo millones con versiones de los Beatles. Motown, el funk y el soul le quitan el público negro a finales de los sesenta.

podcast.title: "Honky Tonk" - Accidental Creation
podcast.body: Bill Doggett's biggest hit, "Honky Tonk," originated entirely by accident at a dance in Lima, Ohio. It started as guitarist Billy Butler's unplanned noodling on his bass strings between songs, which captivated the audience and led the band to improvise around the riff. "Honky Tongue Parts 1 and 2 came about almost by accident."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Audience Demand for "Honky Tonk"
podcast.body: After the spontaneous creation of "Honky Tonk," an audience member requested "that hot new song," prompting the band to recreate it from memory. The crowd's enthusiastic response led them to play the improvised tune ten times by the end of the night. "But then, a couple of songs later, someone in the audience came up and asked them if they could play that hot new song they'd been playing before, again, not realizing it had just been a spur of the moment jam."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Continued Touring Success
podcast.body: Despite being dropped by King Records, Bill Doggett remained a prolific working musician, touring the oldies circuit and performing hundreds of shows a year until his death in 1996 at age 80. "Doggett's spent most of the rest of his life, touring the oldies circuit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: De Facto Musical Director for Lucky Millinder
podcast.body: Bill Doggett served as the unofficial musical director for Lucky Millinder's band during his tenure as pianist. Millinder, unable to play an instrument, relied on musicians like Doggett to create arrangements. "Doggert was, from what I can tell, the de facto musical director for Melinda's band in this period."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Desire for Originality with Honking Saxophone
podcast.body: After a couple of years playing in an organ trio and being compared to Wild Bill Davis, Bill Doggett decided to differentiate his sound. He brought in a "honking saxophone player" to take the lead instrumental role, with Doggett focusing on rhythmic support, leading to his unique sound. "And so, to vary the style, he decided to take on a hunking saxophone player to be the group's lead instrumentalist, while Dogget would concentrate on providing a rhythmic pad."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Band Leader
podcast.body: In his late teens, after moving to New York from Philadelphia (where he was born in 1916), Bill Doggett formed his own band, where he played the piano. "Doggert was born in 1916 in Philadelphia, and he moved to New York in his late teens and formed his own band, for which he was the piano player."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Early Work with Millinder
podcast.body: Bill Doggett worked with Lucky Millinder before going on to join the Ink Spots' backing band. "He'd worked with Bill Doggett before Doggett went off to join the ink spots backing band."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 7: "Good Rockin' Tonight" by Wynonie Harris

podcast.title: Extensive Work as Arranger/Pianist
podcast.body: After leaving The Ink Spots, Bill Doggett became Ella Fitzgerald's full-time arranger and pianist for a couple of years, then moved to Illinois Jacquet's band in the same role, demonstrating his high demand and versatile skills. "Dogget moved over full-time to become Ella's Aranger and Peanest."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: King Records Dropping Doggett Over Royalty Dispute
podcast.body: Bill Doggett's career as a charting artist largely ceased after 1960 when he asked King Records' Sid Nathan for a higher royalty rate, given the millions his recordings had generated for the label. King Records responded by dropping him from their roster. "Doggett's spent most of the rest of his life, touring the oldies circuit."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Lifelong Dedication to "Honky Tonk"
podcast.body: Bill Doggett consistently played "Honky Tonk" at every single one of his shows throughout his life, understanding its importance to his audience and his identity as an artist. "I just wouldn't be Bill Doggett if I didn't play Hanky Tonk. That's what the people pay to hear, so that's what they get."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Louis Jordan's Musical Director
podcast.body: Bill Doggett became the sole pianist and effectively the musical director for Louis Jordan's band, one of the biggest R&B groups of the era, after initially alternating duties with Wild Bill Davis. "Dogget once again basically became the musical director for one of the biggest bands in the R&B business."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Millinder's Pianist
podcast.body: Bill Doggett, the piano player in Lucky Millinder's band, asserted that it was Millinder's own idea, not Mo Gale's, to recruit Sister Rosetta Tharp. "But Bill Doggett, the piano player with Melinda's band, said that it was Melinda's idea, not Gale's, to get Tharp on board."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
srcs.episode: Episode 5: "This Train" by Sister Rosetta Tharpe

podcast.title: Pivotal in Genre Transition (Swing to R&B)
podcast.body: Bill Doggett was an important part of Lucky Millinder's band, which was pivotal in the transition of popular music from swing to R&B. He helped set up the band's style, making it suitable for future R&B vocalists. "The Melinda band were pivotal in the move from swing music to R and B, and Doggert was an important part in that move."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Recognized as De Facto Ink Spots Member
podcast.body: Although primarily a side-man and arranger for The Ink Spots for two years, Bill Doggett was so integral to the group's sound and success during their classic lineup that he is now included in lists of proper members by band historians. "While he was a side-man, rather than a full member of the group, he was important enough to them that he now gets counted in lists of proper members put together by historians of the band."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Reputation Untarnished After Millinder Departure
podcast.body: The reasons for Bill Doggett's departure from Lucky Millinder's band are unknown, but it didn't negatively impact his career. He remained managed by Mo Gale, who then placed him with The Ink Spots. "it can't have been anything that put a stain on his reputation, because Doggert remained with Melinda's manager, Mo Gillespie."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs

podcast.title: Shift from Piano to Hammond Organ Trio
podcast.body: Inspired by Wild Bill Davis's pioneering work, Bill Doggett left Louis Jordan's band to form his own organ trio, adopting the Hammond organ as his primary instrument and recording blues tracks in a similar style to Davis. "When Dogget left Jordan's band, he decided to form an organ trio, just like Davis's."

srcs.source: A History of Rock Music in 500 Songs
